sermon:
## The Open House
*What love looks like when it has to find a bed by nightfall*

**Text:** 3 John 1-8 · **Supporting:** Matthew 25:35; Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2; Matthew 10:40-42

We have learned to measure a church by what it believes. The statement of faith on the website, the doctrine printed in the bulletin, the position held on the contested questions of the hour. All of it real, all of it good. And all of it possible to keep with the front door locked. The shortest of John's letters refuses that measurement. It does not ask Gaius what he affirms. It asks the apostle's coworkers who came through town tired and hungry whether anyone took them in. The truth in this letter is not a thing you sign. It is a thing you host.

**The man John commends, and what he is commended for**

John writes to one man and he loves him plainly. "The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth." Then the line everyone half-remembers and almost no one reads in context: "Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, as it goes well with your soul" (3 John 2). It has been printed on prosperity cards and read over offering plates as a promise of money and muscle. Read it where it sits. It is a greeting. John's hope for his friend's body is no larger than his confidence about his friend's soul, and his confidence about his friend's soul is the engine of the whole letter. Because what comes next is not a wish. It is a report. "I rejoiced greatly when the brothers came and testified to your truth, as indeed you are walking in the truth" (3 John 3). Brothers came through. They went on. And they told the old apostle what they had found in Gaius's house.

What had they found. Strangers received. "Beloved, it is a faithful thing you do in all your efforts for these brothers, strangers as they are" (3 John 5). Not friends of long standing. Not the home crowd. Men he had never met, carrying letters and a Name, knocking after dark. And Gaius fed them, housed them, and then did the thing the letter actually turns on: he sent them on. "You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God" (3 John 6). The road was the gospel's only infrastructure in the first century, and a traveling teacher with no bed and no bread did not get to the next town. Gaius was the bed. Gaius was the bread. The truth got down the road because one man's house was open.

**The reason it counts as more than kindness**

Here is where the letter stops being a thank-you note and becomes theology. John tells us why these men were on the road in the first place. "For they have gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles" (3 John 7). For the sake of the Name. They would not take support from the pagans they preached to, because the gospel cannot be a thing you sell to the people you are trying to save. So the mission had only one place to land for its supply: the church. The believers down the road. The open house.

And John names the stakes in the next breath. "Therefore we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth" (3 John 8). Fellow workers. The Greek is synergoi, the same word Paul uses for the people laboring beside him in the gospel. The man who never preached a sermon, never crossed a sea, never stood before a hostile crowd, is counted a coworker in the mission because he opened a door and filled a plate. This is not a metaphor. John is saying that the kingdom does not finally distinguish between the one who carries the Name and the one who carries the supper. The reward Jesus promised lands on both. "The one who receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet's reward" (Matthew 10:41). Same reward. Different hands.

Which means hospitality in this letter is not a soft virtue we tuck under the harder ones. It is the truth in its bodily form. "I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth" (3 John 4), John writes, and the walking he is rejoicing over is a man making up a bed. Scripture keeps fusing these two things that we keep prying apart. "Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality" (Romans 12:13). "Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" (Hebrews 13:2). The Lord himself sets the final exam there: "I was a stranger and you welcomed me" (Matthew 25:35). Not, you held the line on doctrine. You welcomed me.

**The seat we would rather keep**

I know how this lands, because I have stood on the wrong side of it. It is possible to run a church that is doctrinally exact and relationally closed. It is possible to be precise about the truth and never once put it on a plate. I have preached the open house and kept my own evenings shut. I have admired Gaius from a pulpit and not been him on a Tuesday, when the knock is inconvenient and the stranger is real and the cost is my quiet and my margin and my home. We did not lose the truth by denying it. We lost it by hosting nobody with it.

And the Name is the reason it cannot stay theoretical. The men on the road went out for the sake of the Name, which is to say for the sake of Christ, who is the truth they carried. He was himself the traveling stranger with no place to lay his head, received by some and refused by others, and he tied his own reception to a cup of cold water given to the least of these. So when Gaius opens the door, he is not running a benevolence program. He is receiving Christ in the form of Christ's servant, the way Christ said he would be received. The whole mission of the Son who went out and was turned away comes down to this small repeated act in believers' houses: somebody opened the door. The supper became the synergy. The bed became the gospel's next mile.

The church is not measured by who agrees with it. It is measured by who it lets in.

Fellow workers, or merely audience.

## Who Has to Be First
*A short letter on the seat at the head of the table*

**Text:** 3 John 9-15 · **Supporting:** Mark 10:42-45; 3 John 11; Matthew 23:6; Philippians 2:3

There are three men in this letter and only one of them is a heretic, and it is none of them. John never accuses Diotrephes of bad doctrine. That is the part that should keep a pastor up at night. The man who tears the church is not wrong about Christ. He is wrong about the seat. He has decided who has to be first, and the answer is himself, and from that small wrong everything else follows, the lies, the locked door, the people put out. You can hold the truth on paper and shut it out of the room. This letter watched a man do exactly that.

**The love of first place, and where it goes**

John states the diagnosis without softening it. "I have written something to the church, but Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first, does not acknowledge our authority" (3 John 9). Who likes to put himself first. The phrasing is almost clinical. It is not that Diotrephes seized power in a crisis or was forced to a hard call. He likes the first place. It is an appetite, and John names it as the root, before he names a single one of its fruits.

Then he names the fruits, and watch the order, because it is the anatomy of every petty tyranny the church has ever produced. First, the talk. "Talking wicked nonsense against us" (3 John 10), the man who has to be first must bring down anyone whose authority outranks his own, and he does it with words, with the running drip of accusation that needs no evidence and never quite says the whole thing out loud. Second, the closed door. "He refuses to welcome the brothers", the same brothers Gaius fed, the workers carrying the Name, turned away at the threshold by a man guarding his seat. Third, the purge. "And also stops those who want to and puts them out of the church." He will not host the missionaries, and he will not let anyone else host them either, and the members who try get shown the door. The love of first place does not stay personal. It builds a structure. It always ends with someone being put out.

This is the oldest sin wearing a churchman's collar. It is the sin Jesus named in the men who "love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues" (Matthew 23:6). It is the precise thing he confronted in his own twelve, when James and John came asking for the seats on his right and his left, and he turned to all of them: "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them. But it shall not be so among you" (Mark 10:42-43). Not so among you. Diotrephes heard that and built a small kingdom anyway. So have I, in the rooms where I had the gavel. The instinct to be first does not announce itself as pride. It arrives dressed as protecting the church, keeping order, holding the line. It rarely feels like ambition while you are doing it.

**The two men John holds up instead**

Against the one who grasps, John sets two who do not. First, a command, planted right in the middle of the letter like a hinge: "Beloved, do not imitate evil but imitate good. Whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God" (3 John 11). Imitate. The whole letter turns on that verb. John is not asking the church to merely disapprove of Diotrephes. He is telling them not to copy him, because what you imitate is what you become, and what you become reveals whose you are. The man who has not seen God is exposed not by his creed but by his conduct in a room with a seat in it.

Then Demetrius, named for one reason. "Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also add our testimony, and you know that our testimony is true" (3 John 12). Three witnesses for one ordinary man. Everyone vouches for him. The truth itself vouches for him, his life and the gospel say the same thing, with no gap between them. And John adds his own. We are never told what Demetrius did. We are told what he was: trusted, by everyone, by the truth, by the apostle. He is the anti-Diotrephes. One man cannot stop talking about himself. The other does not have to say anything, because everyone else is already saying it for him. That is the only kind of greatness this letter recognizes, and it is the kind that never asks for the seat.

**The seat you have to refuse**

The self-implication here is total, and I will not pretend I stand outside it. Every leader is a Diotrephes in waiting. The longer you hold a pulpit, a board, a household, the more the seat begins to feel like yours, the more dissent begins to feel like disloyalty, the more your preference begins to feel like the church's good. We do not usually fall by denying Christ. We fall by needing to be first and calling it stewardship. The locked door is not a doctrine. It is a temperament, and it is mine on my worst days.

And the reason the seat has to be refused is the Name. The brothers Diotrephes turned away had gone out for the sake of the Name, accepting nothing, carrying Christ to the road. The truth Demetrius was vouched for by is the same truth those workers served. Christ is the Name and the truth both, and he is the one who, having every right to the first place, took the last one. "The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). He had the only seat that was rightfully his and he got up from it and went to a cross. So the man who has to be first in the church is not merely difficult. He is imitating the wrong master. He is doing the exact thing Christ undid. To refuse the seat is not modesty. It is following the One who emptied himself, "counting others more significant than yourselves" (Philippians 2:3), to the only throne that was ever real, which turned out to be wood and nails.

The letter ends with peace and friends greeted by name. "Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends, every one of them" (3 John 15). Every one of them. The open house, one more time, against the locked door.

Imitate the good. Refuse the seat.
